title: Genes Date a Split Without Fossils

scenes.tts: Two living species may have left no fossil of the moment they split. Can their genes still tell you when it happened? Line up the same gene from both. They differ at some sites. Those differences are a record, and a record can be read as time.
scenes.visual: Two tips, a split node marked with a question, a crossed-out fossil; two gene strips with a few highlighted differing sites.
scenes.narration: Two living species may have left no fossil of the moment they split. Can their genes still tell you when it happened? Line up the same gene from both. They differ at some sites. Those differences are a record, and a record can be read as time.

scenes.tts: When one population splits into two lineages, each keeps gaining mutations. Some spread until every member of the lineage carries them. Each of those is a substitution. Substitutions pile up along both branches, starting at the common ancestor. So the distance between the two tips is the rate times the time, twice over. Write it as D equals two r t.

Substitutions pile up along both branches, starting at the common ancestor. So the distance between the two tips is the rate times the time, twice over. Write it as D = 2rt.
scenes.visual: Tree grows from the ancestor; substitution ticks appear on both branches; braces r t on each branch; the formula D = rt + rt = 2rt.

scenes.tts: There is a catch. A site can change twice, or change and change back. Then you see fewer differences than really happened. So the share of sites that differ undercounts the change. Say thirty percent of sites differ. The corrected distance is zero point three eight three substitutions per site. That is more than a quarter more change than you can see.

scenes.visual: One site square changes and changes back; two bars, observed 0.30 and corrected 0.383 computed from the formula, the extra part outlined as unseen change.

scenes.tts: Sequences alone cannot separate rate from time. A distance of zero point zero two could mean a fast rate over a short time. It could mean a slow rate over a long time. You need an age from outside the sequences. The commonest is a fossil. Suppose two species are known from fossils to have split three million years ago. Their corrected distance is zero point zero one two. Divide by twice three million years, and the rate is two times ten to the minus nine substitutions per site per year.
scenes.caption: Sequences alone cannot separate rate from time. A distance of 0.02 could mean a fast rate over a short time. It could mean a slow rate over a long time. You need an age from outside the sequences. The commonest is a fossil. Suppose two species are known from fossils to have split 3 million years ago. Their corrected distance is 0.012. Divide by twice 3 million years, and the rate is 2 × 10⁻⁹ substitutions per site per year.

scenes.tts: Now take a second pair, in the same gene. Their corrected distance is zero point zero two four. Divide by twice the rate. The answer is six million years. Check it. Twice the rate, times six million years, gives zero point zero two four. The common error is to forget the factor of two. That gives twelve million years, which is wrong.

scenes.tts: One caution remains. The oldest fossil shows the group existed by then. So it gives a minimum age. The real split was earlier, by an unknown margin. Both dates may be older than these figures. These dates also assume equal, constant rates and an exact calibration. Even with abundant data, a date stays sensitive to its assumptions. So keep this rule. A clock needs a calibration, and a fossil gives only a minimum age.
